doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Nola Studio and the Ralph Flanagan audition
summary: Hanging around Nola Studio, he auditioned for Ralph Flanagan by bluffing his way past the line, played the fifth baritone part and got the job.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: That’s right. I just let him — see I used to go up to Nola Studio where all the bands rehearsed.
Oh yes. A lot of people have mentioned that.

Yeah. We just used to hang around there looking at — you’d see Benny Goodman rehearsing, you’d see Artie Shaw rehearsing, you’d see Tommy Dorsey rehearsing. And there was Shep Fields rehearsing. Well I said what harm could this do? And there was a sign out there, we need a baritone sax and bass clarinet players, so fine, boom, I sat down in the chair and played. Oh good, what’s your name kid? And that’s how I got with Ralph Flanagan. I finally graduated high school and then they held the auditions, and word got around in all the studios, all the music student studios. So and so was holding auditions next Thursday at four o’clock. And so and so next Monday at one o’clock at the Hartnet Studio owner. And they said well Ralph Flanagan is holding auditions down at Manhattan Center on 34th Street at four o’clock on Thursday, which was true. So I brought my instruments down and there was a line of maybe 25, 30 guys, there was a line. You know, “next.” So I saw this line and I just walked right up to them and I said, “Who’s the manager?” “Oh that guy there, George Thompson.” And, “Are you Mr.

Thompson?” He said, “Yes I am.” I said, “My name is Kenny Davern and I can’t wait this line, you see I have a gig” — which I was lying through my teeth — “I have to be at a gig in about 45 minutes and I wonder if it would be possible for me to—” He said, “Okay.” And he took me in. Well there in back of the screen was Ralph Flanagan putzing around on the piano and a bass player and a drummer. And he puts up the sheet music and I take out my horn. It was the fifth baritone part, which was like minor seconds to the lead all the way through.

Exactly, right. Up in the high register. No problem with that. In the alto, the fifth part on alto was also like the joke. “What kind of harmony does he play?” “He plays the fifth alto part.” So I did that and I found out that Ralph’s theme song was “Moonlight Serenade,” because it was a Glenn Miller type band, it was “Moonlight Serenade” the other way around. Upside down. Like “Moonlight Serenade” [humms]. Well this was [humms]. And you had to do this whole thing in one big breath, and it was a long son of a gun you know. Took a deep breath and I played all the way up in the high register, okay, fine. And then, “Next.” He sat down, “Well play ‘Muskrat Ramble’ okay B flat.” And we played that, and we played “That’s A Plenty.” “Okay, we’ll let you know.” You know, pack it up, boomp.
And then you went to your supposed gig.

Yeah then I went to my supposed gig, which I went up to my friend in Queens house and had dinner and that night the telephone rings about nine o’clock, my mother calling my friend’s house. She says, “You better get home right away.” “Why?” “You’re leaving at twelve noon from in front of the President Hotel tomorrow.” Well woomp — away I went. And about three months later or four months later I came back, like if I went out weighing 130 pounds, I came back 116.
